claim: Multipotent intestinal stem cells (ISCs) are responsible for tissue homeostasis in the adult Drosophila midgut.
source: Multipotent intestinal stem cells (ISCs) are responsible for tissue homeostasis in the adult Drosophila midgut (Jiang and Edgar, 2011; Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Jiang and Edgar, 2011; Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006).

claim: The activity of ISC proliferation and differentiation increases upon tissue damage in the Drosophila midgut.
source: Similar to the mammalian digestive epithelium, the activity of ISC proliferation and differentiation increases upon tissue damage (Amcheslavsky et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Amcheslavsky et al., 2009.

claim: Signaling pathways controlling ISC activity, such as Ras/MAPK, Hippo/Yki, and JAK/Stat, play critical roles in gut homeostasis.
source: Although signaling pathways controlling ISC activity, such as Ras/MAPK (Jiang et al., 2011), Hippo/Yki (Karpowicz et al., 2010; Shaw et al., 2010), and JAK/Stat (Jiang et al., 2009), play critical roles in gut homeostasis, the mechanisms modulating these pathways under different physiological and pathological conditions are not well understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies: Jiang et al., 2011 for Ras/MAPK; Karpowicz et al., 2010 and Shaw et al., 2010 for Hippo/Yki; and Jiang et al., 2009 for JAK/Stat.

claim: It is unclear how ISCs sense microenvironment signals under tissue damage conditions to upregulate the activity of mitogenic pathways such as Ras/MAPK.
source: In particular, it is unclear how ISCs sense microenvironment signals under tissue damage conditions to upregulate the activity of mitogenic pathways such as Ras/MAPK.
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap identified by the authors based on the current state of the field.

claim: The concentration of reactive oxygen species (ROS) is emerging as a critical microenvironment signal that regulates stem cell activity in neuronal and glial progenitors.
source: The concentration of reactive oxygen species (ROS) is emerging as a critical microenvironment signal that regulates stem cell activity in neuronal and glial progenitors (Liu et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2000; Tsatmali et al., 2005), as well as in mammalian hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) (Tothova et al., 2007) and Drosophila hematopoietic progenitors (Owusu-Ansah and Banerjee, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies: Liu et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2000; Tsatmali et al., 2005 for neuronal and glial progenitors; Tothova et al., 2007 for mammalian HSCs; and Owusu-Ansah and Banerjee, 2009 for Drosophila hematopoietic progenitors.

claim: High ROS concentration stimulates, at least in the short term, the activity of stem cells by driving them out of an otherwise quiescent status.
source: In most cases, high ROS concentration stimulates, at least in the short term, the activity of stem cells by driving them out of an otherwise quiescent status.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from the field as indicated by the preceding citations.

claim: Oxidative stress is associated with intestine damage and inflammatory bowel disease in mammals.
source: In mammals, oxidative stress is associated with intestine damage and inflammatory bowel disease (Rezaie et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rezaie et al., 2007.

claim: High ROS levels are produced in response to different types of tissue damage in the Drosophila midgut.
source: In the Drosophila midgut, high ROS levels are produced in response to different types of tissue damage (Ha et al., 2005; Hochmuth et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three studies: Ha et al., 2005; Hochmuth et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2013.

claim: Oxidants such as paraquat and hydrogen peroxide are commonly used to induce tissue damage in Drosophila.
source: Moreover, oxidants such as paraquat and hydrogen peroxide are commonly used to induce tissue damage (Chatterjee and Ip, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chatterjee and Ip, 2009.

claim: High ROS levels in ISCs are sufficient to trigger ISC proliferation.
source: Although high ROS levels in ISCs are sufficient to trigger ISC proliferation (Hochmuth et al., 2011), the connection between oxidative stress and mitogenic signals in ISCs remains obscure.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hochmuth et al., 2011.

claim: The connection between oxidative stress and mitogenic signals in ISCs remains obscure.
source: Although high ROS levels in ISCs are sufficient to trigger ISC proliferation (Hochmuth et al., 2011), the connection between oxidative stress and mitogenic signals in ISCs remains obscure.
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap identified by the authors.

claim: An in vivo RNAi screen was performed to identify novel components required for ISC proliferation in response to tissue damage.
source: We performed an in vivo RNAi screen to identify novel components required for ISC proliferation in response to tissue damage.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental approach taken by the authors.

claim: TRPA1 and RyR were identified as two cation channels required for ISC self-renewal and damage-induced proliferation.
source: In the screen, we identified two cation channels, transient receptor potential A1 (TRPA1) and ryanodine receptor (RyR), which are required for ISC self-renewal and damage-induced proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results of the RNAi screen described in the manuscript.

claim: TRPA1 and RyR are required for Ca2+ homeostasis in ISCs.
source: We show that these channels are required for Ca2+ homeostasis in ISCs and mediate increases in cytosolic Ca2+ in response to oxidative stress and ISC proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging experiments presented in the manuscript (Figure 5).

claim: TRPA1 and RyR mediate increases in cytosolic Ca2+ in response to oxidative stress and ISC proliferation.
source: We show that these channels are required for Ca2+ homeostasis in ISCs and mediate increases in cytosolic Ca2+ in response to oxidative stress and ISC proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging experiments with paraquat treatment presented in the manuscript (Figure 5).

claim: High cytosolic Ca2+ in ISCs can stimulate proliferation.
source: Our results are consistent with a recent study (Deng et al., 2015) showing that high cytosolic Ca2+ in ISCs can stimulate proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Deng et al., 2015.

claim: Ras/MAPK mediates the effects of Ca2+ on ISC proliferation.
source: Finally, we characterize the signaling events downstream of cytosolic Ca2+ increase and demonstrate that Ras/MAPK mediates the effects of Ca2+ on ISC proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic epistasis experiments and dpErk staining presented in the manuscript (Figures 6 and 7).

claim: Ca2+ signaling is required for oxidative stress-induced activation of the Ras/MAPK pathway.
source: Characterization of TRPA1 and RyR demonstrates that Ca2+ signaling is required for oxidative stress-induced activation of the Ras/MAPK pathway, which in turns drives ISC proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by dpErk staining experiments showing that trpA1 RNAi blocks MAPK activation (Figure 6).

claim: TRPA1 is a Ca2+-permeable cation influx channel.
source: TRPA1 is a Ca2+-permeable cation influx channel (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2013.

claim: RyR is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER) cation channel that releases ER Ca2+ into the cytosol.
source: RyR is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER) cation channel that releases ER Ca2+ into the cytosol (Santulli and Marks, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Santulli and Marks, 2015.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of either trpA1 or RyR in adult ISCs completely blocked proliferation induced by paraquat or bleomycin.
source: RNAi-mediated knockdown of either trpA1 or RyR in adult ISCs completely blocked proliferation induced by the tissue-damaging agent paraquat or bleomycin (Figure 1A–C and A'-C', G).
evidence: This claim is supported by pH3 staining data shown in Figure 1A-C, A'-C', and quantified in Figure 1G.

claim: Depletion of trpA1 or RyR causes a gradual loss of the stem cell population, with a significant decrease in esg+ cell density undetectable until 7 days of RNAi expression.
source: Depletion of trpA1 or RyR causes a gradual loss of the stem cell population, with a significant decrease in esg+ cell density undetectable until 7 days of RNAi expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of esg+ cell density shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The RNAi lines do not cause stem cell apoptosis.
source: The RNAi lines do not cause stem cell apoptosis, because cell death cannot be detected with anti-cleaved-caspase 3 staining in the midgut (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C), and the anti-apoptotic gene p35 (Hay et al., 1994) cannot rescue the mitosis defect caused by trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–I,D'–I').
evidence: This claim is supported by cleaved-caspase 3 staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C) and p35 rescue experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–I,D'–I'), along with a citation to Hay et al., 1994 for p35.

claim: Mitosis activity in stem cells expressing trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi can be regained by forced cytosolic calcium influx with RNAi against SERCA.
source: In contrast, mitosis activity in stem cells expressing trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi can be regained by forced cytosolic calcium influx with RNAi against SERCA (Figure 1D–G), an ER Ca2+ ATPase whose inhibition triggers Stim/Orai channel (SOC)-mediated Ca2+ entry into the cytosol (Clapham, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by pH3 staining data shown in Figure 1D–G and a citation to Clapham, 2007 for SERCA function.

claim: These results place cytosolic calcium signaling genetically downstream of TRPA1 and RyR during ISC proliferation.
source: Altogether, these results place cytosolic calcium signaling genetically downstream of TRPA1 and RyR during ISC proliferation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the genetic epistasis experiments showing SERCA RNAi can rescue trpA1 or RyR RNAi phenotypes.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of trpA1 or RyR in adult ISCs suppressed damage-induced proliferation.
source: Consistent with the results obtained with RNAi, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of trpA1 or RyR in adult ISCs suppressed damage-induced proliferation (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by mitosis quantification data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Inhibition of ISC proliferation by trpA1 RNAi is associated with a shortening in midgut length.
source: In addition, at the organ level, inhibition of ISC proliferation by trpA1 RNAi is associated with a shortening in midgut length (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by midgut length measurements shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Wild-type midguts maintain their proper length after feeding paraquat or bleomycin for 2 days.
source: Further, while wild-type midguts maintain their proper length after feeding paraquat or bleomycin for 2 days, midguts with trpA1 RNAi expression in the ISCs exhibit accelerated shortening following tissue damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by midgut length measurements shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Midguts with trpA1 RNAi expression in the ISCs exhibit accelerated shortening following tissue damage.
source: Further, while wild-type midguts maintain their proper length after feeding paraquat or bleomycin for 2 days, midguts with trpA1 RNAi expression in the ISCs exhibit accelerated shortening following tissue damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by midgut length measurements shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The damage-induced midgut shortening phenotype is reminiscent to the gut phenotype observed after depletion of the esg+ cell population when the cell death gene reaper (rpr) is expressed in ISCs for 4 days.
source: This damage-induced midgut shortening phenotype is reminiscent to the gut phenotype observed after depletion of the esg+ cell population when the cell death gene reaper (rpr) is expressed in ISCs for 4 days (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting the importance of ISC activity for maintaining tissue size.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with rpr expression experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: ISC activity is important for maintaining tissue size.
source: This damage-induced midgut shortening phenotype is reminiscent to the gut phenotype observed after depletion of the esg+ cell population when the cell death gene reaper (rpr) is expressed in ISCs for 4 days (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting the importance of ISC activity for maintaining tissue size.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that ISC depletion leads to midgut shortening.

claim: The trpA1 gene is expressed as multiple mRNAs, four of which have been characterized previously.
source: The trpA1 gene is expressed as multiple mRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), four of which have been characterized previously (Zhong et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a diagram in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and a citation to Zhong et al., 2012.

claim: TRPA1-C and -D isoforms are expressed in the midgut.
source: Compared to the TRPA1-A and -B isoforms, expressed in the fly head, TRPA1-C and -D isoforms are expressed in the midgut (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and have different N-terminal residues that might confer sensitivity to different stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TRPA1-A and -B isoforms are expressed in the fly head.
source: Compared to the TRPA1-A and -B isoforms, expressed in the fly head, TRPA1-C and -D isoforms are expressed in the midgut (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and have different N-terminal residues that might confer sensitivity to different stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TRPA1-C and -D isoforms have different N-terminal residues that might confer sensitivity to different stimuli.
source: Compared to the TRPA1-A and -B isoforms, expressed in the fly head, TRPA1-C and -D isoforms are expressed in the midgut (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and have different N-terminal residues that might confer sensitivity to different stimuli.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on structural differences between isoforms.

claim: TRPA1 appears to be expressed in stem cells based on anti-TRPA1 staining.
source: Based on anti-TRPA1 staining, TRPA1 appears to be expressed in stem cells (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A–B.

claim: trpA1 expression can be detected in stem cells in the anterior region of the posterior midgut using a Gal4 fused to the C terminal of trpA1 transcripts via CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in.
source: Using a Gal4 fused to the C terminal of trpA1 transcripts via CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in at the endogenous locus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we could also detect trpA1 expression in stem cells in the anterior region of the posterior midgut (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by trpA1Gal4CP2A expression data shown in Figure 3C and the knock-in strategy shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Stem cell depletion reduces trpA1 total mRNA expression in the midgut by more than 50%.
source: Consistently, stem cell depletion reduces trpA1 total mRNA expression in the midgut by more than 50% (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: TRPA1-C has been identified to regulate defecation of food-borne pathogens in the EEs.
source: In a recent study, for example, TRPA1-C has been identified to regulate defecation of food-borne pathogens in the EEs (Du et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Du et al., 2016.

claim: TRPA1 is mainly required in ISCs for proliferation.
source: However, TRPA1 is mainly required in ISCs for proliferation, because knockdown of trpA1 in self-renewing ISCs, rather than in differentiating ISCs (Su(H)Gbe+ cells, also called enteroblasts (EBs)) or visceral muscles, blocks damage-induced proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-type-specific RNAi experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: TRPA1 protein functions in the stem cells.
source: Further, an additional piece of evidence that TRPA1 protein functions in the stem cells comes from the ex vivo calcium-imaging experiments with GCamP6f reporter, for which the intensity of green fluorescence indicates cytosolic calcium levels (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging experiments and a citation to Chen et al., 2013 for the GCaMP6f reporter.

claim: The TRPA1 agonist AITC can induce calcium influx in ISCs carrying a wild-type allele of trpA1.
source: While the TRPA1 agonist AITC (allyl isothiocyanate (Bautista et al., 2005) can induce calcium influx in ISCs carrying a wild-type allele of trpA1, such response is abolished in flies losing both alleles of wild-type trpA1 (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3E–F and a citation to Bautista et al., 2005 for AITC.

claim: The calcium response to AITC is abolished in flies losing both alleles of wild-type trpA1.
source: While the TRPA1 agonist AITC (allyl isothiocyanate (Bautista et al., 2005) can induce calcium influx in ISCs carrying a wild-type allele of trpA1, such response is abolished in flies losing both alleles of wild-type trpA1 (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3E–F.

claim: RyR appears to be ubiquitously expressed at low levels in the midgut epithelium based on the expression pattern of RyRGal4R14G09.
source: RyR appears to be ubiquitously expressed at low levels in the midgut epithelium, based on the expression pattern of RyRGal4R14G09 (Figure 3D), where Gal4 is under the control of 2.92 kb putative enhancer region sequence of RyR (Pfeiffer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by RyRGal4R14G09 expression data shown in Figure 3D and a citation to Pfeiffer et al., 2008.

claim: Oxidative stress has previously been observed in tissue damage conditions involving JNK activation.
source: Oxidative stress has previously been observed in tissue damage conditions involving JNK activation (Hochmuth et al., 2011) and pathogen infection (Ha et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hochmuth et al., 2011 for JNK activation and Ha et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2013 for pathogen infection.

claim: Oxidative stress has previously been observed in tissue damage conditions involving pathogen infection.
source: Oxidative stress has previously been observed in tissue damage conditions involving JNK activation (Hochmuth et al., 2011) and pathogen infection (Ha et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ha et al., 2005 and Lee et al., 2013.

claim: The source of oxidative stress is generally attributed to an imbalance in the formation of ROS and impaired antioxidant machinery in unhealthy tissues.
source: The source of oxidative stress is generally attributed to an imbalance in the formation of ROS and impaired antioxidant machinery in unhealthy tissues (Hochmuth et al., 2011; Lih-Brody et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hochmuth et al., 2011 and Lih-Brody et al., 1996.

claim: ROS levels in the midgut increase following tissue damage induced by feeding flies with paraquat.
source: Staining with dihydro-ethidium (DHE) (Owusu-Ansah et al., 2008) confirmed that ROS levels in the midgut increase following tissue damage induced by feeding flies with paraquat (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), a widely used oxidant that interferes with electron transfer to catalyze formation of superoxide-free radicals (Bus and Gibson, 1984), or bleomycin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), a chemotherapy drug that cleaves DNA via an unresolved mechanism potentially related to ROS production (Hecht, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by DHE staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and citations to Owusu-Ansah et al., 2008 for DHE method and Bus and Gibson, 1984 for paraquat mechanism.

claim: Paraquat is a widely used oxidant that interferes with electron transfer to catalyze formation of superoxide-free radicals.
source: Staining with dihydro-ethidium (DHE) (Owusu-Ansah et al., 2008) confirmed that ROS levels in the midgut increase following tissue damage induced by feeding flies with paraquat (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), a widely used oxidant that interferes with electron transfer to catalyze formation of superoxide-free radicals (Bus and Gibson, 1984), or bleomycin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), a chemotherapy drug that cleaves DNA via an unresolved mechanism potentially related to ROS production (Hecht, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bus and Gibson, 1984.

claim: ROS levels in the midgut increase following tissue damage induced by feeding flies with bleomycin.
source: Staining with dihydro-ethidium (DHE) (Owusu-Ansah et al., 2008) confirmed that ROS levels in the midgut increase following tissue damage induced by feeding flies with paraquat (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), a widely used oxidant that interferes with electron transfer to catalyze formation of superoxide-free radicals (Bus and Gibson, 1984), or bleomycin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), a chemotherapy drug that cleaves DNA via an unresolved mechanism potentially related to ROS production (Hecht, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by DHE staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and a citation to Hecht, 2000 for bleomycin mechanism.

claim: Bleomycin is a chemotherapy drug that cleaves DNA via an unresolved mechanism potentially related to ROS production.
source: Staining with dihydro-ethidium (DHE) (Owusu-Ansah et al., 2008) confirmed that ROS levels in the midgut increase following tissue damage induced by feeding flies with paraquat (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), a widely used oxidant that interferes with electron transfer to catalyze formation of superoxide-free radicals (Bus and Gibson, 1984), or bleomycin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), a chemotherapy drug that cleaves DNA via an unresolved mechanism potentially related to ROS production (Hecht, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hecht, 2000.

claim: Induction of midgut stress by JNK pathway activation can lead to increased ROS and ISC expansion.
source: In addition, induction of midgut stress by JNK pathway activation or massive EC apoptosis by rpr expression can also lead to increased ROS and ISC expansion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by DHE staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–J.

claim: Induction of midgut stress by massive EC apoptosis by rpr expression can lead to increased ROS and ISC expansion.
source: In addition, induction of midgut stress by JNK pathway activation or massive EC apoptosis by rpr expression can also lead to increased ROS and ISC expansion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by DHE staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–J.

claim: Both TRPA1 and RyR are associated with redox sensing.
source: Both TRPA1 and RyR are associated with redox sensing (Guntur et al., 2015; Hamilton and Reid, 2000; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guntur et al., 2015; Hamilton and Reid, 2000; Sun et al., 2011.

claim: TRPA1-C and TRPA1-D isoforms are H2O2-sensitive.
source: Guntur et al. found that TRPA1-C and TRPA1-D isoforms are H2O2-sensitive and that their endogenous expressions in the ring gland, or ectopic expression in other tissues, confer UV light sensitivity via sensing UV light-induced H2O2 production.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to findings from Guntur et al.

claim: Endogenous expression of TRPA1-C and TRPA1-D in the ring gland confers UV light sensitivity via sensing UV light-induced H2O2 production.
source: Guntur et al. found that TRPA1-C and TRPA1-D isoforms are H2O2-sensitive and that their endogenous expressions in the ring gland, or ectopic expression in other tissues, confer UV light sensitivity via sensing UV light-induced H2O2 production.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to findings from Guntur et al.

claim: Ectopic expression of TRPA1-C and TRPA1-D in other tissues confers UV light sensitivity via sensing UV light-induced H2O2 production.
source: Guntur et al. found that TRPA1-C and TRPA1-D isoforms are H2O2-sensitive and that their endogenous expressions in the ring gland, or ectopic expression in other tissues, confer UV light sensitivity via sensing UV light-induced H2O2 production.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to findings from Guntur et al.

claim: Two-electrode voltage clamp recordings were used to measure the channel activities of TRPA1-C and -D.
source: To directly measure whether gut-specific TRPA1 isoforms can respond to paraquat, we used two-electrode voltage clamp recordings to measure the channel activities of TRPA1-C and -D (Wagner et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental method used, with a citation to Wagner et al., 2000.

claim: TRPA1-C barely displayed any response to paraquat.
source: TRPA1-C barely displayed any response to paraquat (Figure 4A), whereas expression of TRPA1-D induced a slow increase in current (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Expression of TRPA1-D induced a slow increase in current in response to paraquat.
source: TRPA1-C barely displayed any response to paraquat (Figure 4A), whereas expression of TRPA1-D induced a slow increase in current (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Overexpression of TRPA1-D, but not TRPA1-C, stimulated ISCs expressing trpA1 RNAi to proliferate in response to paraquat.
source: Consistently, overexpression of TRPA1-D, but not TRPA1-C, stimulated ISCs expressing trpA1 RNAi to proliferate in response to paraquat (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by pH3 staining data shown in Figure 4C–F (note: text says Figure 3C–F but this appears to be a typo).

claim: trpA1 RNAi suppresses the hyper-proliferation status induced by CncC RNAi.
source: Previously, it has been reported that knockdown of antioxidant protein CncC in ISCs can induce mitosis (Hochmuth et al., 2011). Our observation that trpA1 RNAi suppresses the hyper-proliferation status induced by CncC RNAi (Figure 4G) places TRPA1 genetically downstream of the pathway controlling ROS for ISC proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by mitosis quantification data shown in Figure 4G and a citation to Hochmuth et al., 2011.

claim: TRPA1 is genetically downstream of the pathway controlling ROS for ISC proliferation.
source: Previously, it has been reported that knockdown of antioxidant protein CncC in ISCs can induce mitosis (Hochmuth et al., 2011). Our observation that trpA1 RNAi suppresses the hyper-proliferation status induced by CncC RNAi (Figure 4G) places TRPA1 genetically downstream of the pathway controlling ROS for ISC proliferation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: Overexpression of TRPA1-D or conventional TRPA1-A isoform in stem cells can induce mitosis significantly.
source: Further, overexpression of TRPA1-D or conventional TRPA1-A isoform (active at 29°C) in stem cells can induce mitosis significantly, suggesting that increased TRPA1-calcium signaling is sufficient to drive ISC proliferation (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by mitosis quantification data shown in Figure 4H (note: text says Figure 4H but may refer to a different panel).

claim: Increased TRPA1-calcium signaling is sufficient to drive ISC proliferation.
source: Further, overexpression of TRPA1-D or conventional TRPA1-A isoform (active at 29°C) in stem cells can induce mitosis significantly, suggesting that increased TRPA1-calcium signaling is sufficient to drive ISC proliferation (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that TRPA1 overexpression induces mitosis.

claim: TRPA1 and RyR are not critically required in the midgut epithelium for development.
source: Interestingly, TRPA1 and RyR are not critically required in the midgut epithelium for development, because flies expressing trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi with esgGal4 throughout development [that is, in adult midgut progenitors (AMPs) during larval stages and in adults ISCs, see (Jiang and Edgar, 2009) can survive to adulthood without gross defects when they are fed with normal food].
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that flies with RNAi expression throughout development survive to adulthood, with a citation to Jiang and Edgar, 2009.

claim: The number of GFP+ (i.e. high cytosolic Ca2+ concentration) ISCs in wild-type midguts increases significantly 10 min after adding paraquat to a final concentration of 4 mM.
source: While the number of GFP+ (i.e. high cytosolic Ca2+ concentration) ISCs in wild-type midguts increases significantly 10 min after adding paraquat to a final concentration of 4 mM (Figure 5A, A' and D), expression of trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi in ISCs (driven by esgGal4 throughout development) not only reduced the basal levels of cytosolic Ca2+ in stem cells (Figure 5A–C) but also inhibited the ROS-mediated increase in cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 5A'–C').
evidence: This claim is supported by GCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 5A, A' and quantified in Figure 5D.

claim: Expression of trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi in ISCs reduced the basal levels of cytosolic Ca2+ in stem cells.
source: While the number of GFP+ (i.e. high cytosolic Ca2+ concentration) ISCs in wild-type midguts increases significantly 10 min after adding paraquat to a final concentration of 4 mM (Figure 5A, A' and D), expression of trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi in ISCs (driven by esgGal4 throughout development) not only reduced the basal levels of cytosolic Ca2+ in stem cells (Figure 5A–C) but also inhibited the ROS-mediated increase in cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 5A'–C').
evidence: This claim is supported by GCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: Expression of trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi in ISCs inhibited the ROS-mediated increase in cytosolic Ca2+.
source: While the number of GFP+ (i.e. high cytosolic Ca2+ concentration) ISCs in wild-type midguts increases significantly 10 min after adding paraquat to a final concentration of 4 mM (Figure 5A, A' and D), expression of trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi in ISCs (driven by esgGal4 throughout development) not only reduced the basal levels of cytosolic Ca2+ in stem cells (Figure 5A–C) but also inhibited the ROS-mediated increase in cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 5A'–C').
evidence: This claim is supported by GCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 5A'–C' and quantified in Figure 5D.

claim: The observed reduction of high Ca2+ ISCs is not due to decrease in the total number of ISCs in young adult flies.
source: The observed reduction of high Ca2+ ISCs is not due to decrease in the total number of ISCs, as total ISC number or density in young adult flies is not yet significantly affected by trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of ISC numbers shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with 4 mM paraquat caused a slow and continuous increase in the average number of high Ca2+ ISCs.
source: Consistent with the TRPA1 channel kinetics as measured in the voltage clamp experiments in oocytes (Figure 4A–B), treatment with 4 mM paraquat caused a slow and continuous increase in the average number of high Ca2+ ISCs (Figure 5E), whereas the TRPA1 agonist AITC triggered a sharp increase followed by a quick drop in the number of high Ca2+ ISCs (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The TRPA1 agonist AITC triggered a sharp increase followed by a quick drop in the number of high Ca2+ ISCs.
source: Consistent with the TRPA1 channel kinetics as measured in the voltage clamp experiments in oocytes (Figure 4A–B), treatment with 4 mM paraquat caused a slow and continuous increase in the average number of high Ca2+ ISCs (Figure 5E), whereas the TRPA1 agonist AITC triggered a sharp increase followed by a quick drop in the number of high Ca2+ ISCs (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Responses to both paraquat and AITC were dependent on TRPA1 and RyR.
source: Finally, responses to both paraquat and AITC were dependent on TRPA1 and RyR (Figure 5E–F), whereas treatment with the SERCA inhibitor thapsigargin, as a positive control, led to increased Ca2+ in ISCs expressing trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5E–F.

claim: Treatment with the SERCA inhibitor thapsigargin led to increased Ca2+ in ISCs expressing trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi.
source: Finally, responses to both paraquat and AITC were dependent on TRPA1 and RyR (Figure 5E–F), whereas treatment with the SERCA inhibitor thapsigargin, as a positive control, led to increased Ca2+ in ISCs expressing trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: trpA1 RNAi blocked the increase of cytosolic Ca2+ following treatment with 2 mM paraquat.
source: Using GCaMP5G as the Ca2+ reporter and tdTomato as an internal control, we found that trpA1 RNAi blocked the increase of cytosolic Ca2+ following treatment with 2 mM paraquat (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,A', B,B').
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,A', B,B'.

claim: The percentage of high Ca2+ ISCs among all stem cells increased from 23% to 63% when flies were fed 2 mM paraquat for 1 day.
source: With TRIC lexGFP and a conventional UAS-RFP reporter, we found that the percentage of high Ca2+ ISCs among all stem cells increased from 23% to 63% (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,C', F) when flies were fed 2 mM paraquat for 1 day.
evidence: This claim is supported by TRIC reporter data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,C', F.

claim: In adult midguts expressing trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi in adult ISCs for 6 days, high Ca2+ ISCs showed little, if any, increase following paraquat feeding.
source: In adult midguts expressing trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi in adult ISCs for 6 days, high Ca2+ ISCs showed little, if any, increase following paraquat feeding (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,D', E,E', F).
evidence: This claim is supported by TRIC reporter data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,D', E,E', F.

claim: Membrane depolarization and Ca2+ influx can activate Ras/MAPK in neurons.
source: The biological functions of TRPA1, RyR, and cytosolic Ca2+ signaling have been extensively studied in neurons, where it has been established that membrane depolarization and Ca2+ influx can activate Ras/MAPK (Randlett et al., 2015a; Rosen et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Randlett et al., 2015a and Rosen et al., 1994.

claim: Adult midguts expressing SERCA RNAi in ISCs for 2 days showed induced MAPK activity.
source: Adult midguts expressing SERCA RNAi in ISCs for 2 days, which at that stage do not present signs of ISCs expansion, showed induced MAPK activity (Figure 6A–B), and expression of trpA1 RNAi (Figure 6C) or RyR RNAi (Figure 6D) decreased the levels of MAPK activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by dpErk staining data shown in Figure 6A–B.

claim: Expression of trpA1 RNAi decreased the levels of MAPK activity induced by SERCA RNAi.
source: Adult midguts expressing SERCA RNAi in ISCs for 2 days, which at that stage do not present signs of ISCs expansion, showed induced MAPK activity (Figure 6A–B), and expression of trpA1 RNAi (Figure 6C) or RyR RNAi (Figure 6D) decreased the levels of MAPK activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by dpErk staining data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Expression of RyR RNAi decreased the levels of MAPK activity induced by SERCA RNAi.
source: Adult midguts expressing SERCA RNAi in ISCs for 2 days, which at that stage do not present signs of ISCs expansion, showed induced MAPK activity (Figure 6A–B), and expression of trpA1 RNAi (Figure 6C) or RyR RNAi (Figure 6D) decreased the levels of MAPK activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by dpErk staining data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: SERCA RNAi could override trpA1 RNAi to activate MAPK.
source: Consistent with our observation that ISC Ca2+ induction by SERCA inhibition does not depend on trpA1 or RyR (Figure 5G), SERCA RNAi could override trpA1 RNAi (Figure 6G) or RyR RNAi (Figure 6H) to activate MAPK.
evidence: This claim is supported by dpErk staining data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: SERCA RNAi could override RyR RNAi to activate MAPK.
source: Consistent with our observation that ISC Ca2+ induction by SERCA inhibition does not depend on trpA1 or RyR (Figure 5G), SERCA RNAi could override trpA1 RNAi (Figure 6G) or RyR RNAi (Figure 6H) to activate MAPK.
evidence: This claim is supported by dpErk staining data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Yki RNAi could inhibit ISC proliferation caused by SERCA RNAi.
source: Although Yki RNAi could inhibit ISC proliferation caused by SERCA RNAi (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–G), it could not block MAPK activity (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by mitosis quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–G.

claim: Yki RNAi could not block MAPK activity induced by SERCA RNAi.
source: Although Yki RNAi could inhibit ISC proliferation caused by SERCA RNAi (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–G), it could not block MAPK activity (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by dpErk staining data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Ras1 RNAi could block SERCA RNAi-induced MAPK activity.
source: On the other hand, Ras1 (Drosophila Ras) RNAi could block SERCA RNAi-induced MAPK activity (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by dpErk staining data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Ras/MAPK activity is likely the direct target of high cytosolic Ca2+ in ISCs, rather than the consequence of cross-activation by other proliferation-related pathways such as Yki.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that Ras/MAPK activity is likely the direct target of high cytosolic Ca2+ in ISCs, rather than the consequence of cross-activation by other proliferation-related pathways such as Yki.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the genetic epistasis experiments showing Yki RNAi does not block MAPK activation by SERCA RNAi.

claim: Paraquat feeding for 1 day led to an increase in the number of cells with high dpErk signals, a majority of which are high Ca2+ ISCs.
source: To further examine the relationship between Ca2+ levels and MAPK activity, we performed dpErk staining of midguts expressing the TRIC reporter in ISCs. Paraquat feeding for 1 day led to an increase in the number of cells with high dpErk signals, a majority of which are high Ca2+ ISCs (Figure 6I,I').
evidence: This claim is supported by dpErk and TRIC reporter co-staining data shown in Figure 6I,I'.

claim: Paraquat induction of MAPK activity appears to require high Ca2+ in ISCs.
source: Moreover, paraquat induction of MAPK activity appears to require high Ca2+ in ISCs, because such response could be inhibited by trpA1 RNAi expression in ISCs (Figure 6J,J').
evidence: This claim is supported by dpErk and TRIC reporter co-staining data shown in Figure 6J,J'.

claim: A common mechanism by which Ca2+ regulates Ras/MAPK in neurons is through Ca2+-sensitive Src kinases.
source: In neurons, a common mechanism by which Ca2+ regulates Ras/MAPK is through Ca2+-sensitive Src kinases (Cullen and Lockyer, 2002), in a process faster than any transcriptional response (Randlett et al., 2015b; Rosen et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cullen and Lockyer, 2002; Randlett et al., 2015b; Rosen et al., 1994.

claim: Overexpression of Src (Src42A or Src64B in Drosophila) in ISCs triggers ectopic MAPK activation and proliferation.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of Src (Src42A or Src64B in Drosophila) in ISCs triggers ectopic MAPK activation and proliferation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C), even in the presence of trpA1 RNAi (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by dpErk staining and mitosis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C, E–H.

claim: Src64B RNAi significantly inhibits SERCA RNAi-induced ISC proliferation.
source: Moreover, we could observe significant inhibition of SERCA RNAi-induced ISC proliferation by Src64B RNAi (Figure 6—figure supplement 2I) despite the likelihood of functional redundancy between Src64B and Src42A (Ma et al., 2013; Tateno et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by mitosis quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2I and citations to Ma et al., 2013 and Tateno et al., 2000.

claim: Src might mediate the activation of Ras/MAPK by cytosolic Ca2+ in ISCs.
source: These data suggest that Src might mediate the activation of Ras/MAPK by cytosolic Ca2+ in ISCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Src overexpression and RNAi experiments.

claim: ISCs expressing the active forms of Ras1, Raf, CanA1, CRTC, and CrebB displayed an hyper-proliferation phenotype.
source: Consistent with previous results (Deng et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2011), ISCs expressing the active forms of many Ca2+ effector proteins, such as Ras1, Raf, phosphatase Calcineurin A1 (CanA1), CREB-regulated transcriptional co-activator (CRTC), and cyclic-AMP response element binding protein B (CrebB), displayed an hyper-proliferation phenotype (Figure 7A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by pH3 staining data shown in Figure 7A–E and citations to Deng et al., 2015 and Jiang et al., 2011.

claim: MAPK activation via expression of active Ras1, constitutively active Raf, or secreted form of spi is epistatic to trpA1 RNAi for ISCs proliferation.
source: Strikingly, MAPK activation via expression of active Ras1 (Ras1A), constitutively active Raf (Rafgof), or secreted form of spi is epistatic to trpA1 RNAi for ISCs proliferation (Figure 7A–B and A'–B', 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by pH3 staining data shown in Figure 7A–B, A'–B' and quantified in Figure 7F.

claim: MAPK activation is epistatic to RyR RNAi.
source: Consistently, MAPK activation is epistatic to RyR RNAi (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by pH3 staining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: trpA1 RNAi effectively blocked the mitogenic activity of constitutively active CanA1.
source: By contrast, trpA1 RNAi effectively blocked the mitogenic activity of constitutively active CanA1 (CanA1ca) (Dijkers and O'Farrell, 2007), CRTC (Kim et al., 2016), or active CrebB (CrebBact) (Ganguly-Fitzgerald et al., 2006) (Figure 7C–E and C'–E', F).
evidence: This claim is supported by pH3 staining data shown in Figure 7C–E, C'–E' and quantified in Figure 7F, with citations to Dijkers and O'Farrell, 2007; Kim et al., 2016; Ganguly-Fitzgerald et al., 2006.

claim: trpA1 RNAi effectively blocked the mitogenic activity of CRTC.
source: By contrast, trpA1 RNAi effectively blocked the mitogenic activity of constitutively active CanA1 (CanA1ca) (Dijkers and O'Farrell, 2007), CRTC (Kim et al., 2016), or active CrebB (CrebBact) (Ganguly-Fitzgerald et al., 2006) (Figure 7C–E and C'–E', F).
evidence: This claim is supported by pH3 staining data shown in Figure 7C–E, C'–E' and quantified in Figure 7F, with citations to Dijkers and O'Farrell, 2007; Kim et al., 2016; Ganguly-Fitzgerald et al., 2006.

claim: trpA1 RNAi effectively blocked the mitogenic activity of active CrebB.
source: By contrast, trpA1 RNAi effectively blocked the mitogenic activity of constitutively active CanA1 (CanA1ca) (Dijkers and O'Farrell, 2007), CRTC (Kim et al., 2016), or active CrebB (CrebBact) (Ganguly-Fitzgerald et al., 2006) (Figure 7C–E and C'–E', F).
evidence: This claim is supported by pH3 staining data shown in Figure 7C–E, C'–E' and quantified in Figure 7F, with citations to Dijkers and O'Farrell, 2007; Kim et al., 2016; Ganguly-Fitzgerald et al., 2006.

claim: Ras1 RNAi could suppress SERCA RNAi-induced ISC proliferation.
source: Furthermore, while Ras1 RNAi could suppress SERCA RNAi-induced ISC proliferation, neither CanA1 RNAi nor CrebB RNAi could (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–G), and CRTC RNAi could only confer moderate suppression of ISC hyper-proliferation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by mitosis quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–G.

claim: Neither CanA1 RNAi nor CrebB RNAi could suppress SERCA RNAi-induced ISC proliferation.
source: Furthermore, while Ras1 RNAi could suppress SERCA RNAi-induced ISC proliferation, neither CanA1 RNAi nor CrebB RNAi could (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–G), and CRTC RNAi could only confer moderate suppression of ISC hyper-proliferation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by mitosis quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–G.

claim: CRTC RNAi could only confer moderate suppression of ISC hyper-proliferation induced by SERCA RNAi.
source: Furthermore, while Ras1 RNAi could suppress SERCA RNAi-induced ISC proliferation, neither CanA1 RNAi nor CrebB RNAi could (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–G), and CRTC RNAi could only confer moderate suppression of ISC hyper-proliferation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by mitosis quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–F.

claim: MAPK activity is both necessary and sufficient for high Ca2+-triggered ISC proliferation.
source: Results of these genetic epistasis analyses, together with examination of changes in pErk signal intensity (Figure 6), indicate that MAPK activity is both necessary and sufficient for high Ca2+-triggered ISC proliferation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the genetic epistasis experiments and dpErk staining data.

claim: EGFR is required for MAPK activity and ISC proliferation.
source: Previous studies have documented that receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) EGFR is required for MAPK activity and ISC proliferation (Jiang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2011.

claim: EGFR RNAi completely inhibited ISCs proliferation caused by SERCA RNAi.
source: We found that EGFR RNAi completely inhibited ISCs proliferation caused by SERCA RNAi (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,F), indicating that MAPK activation by Ca2+ requires EGFR signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by mitosis quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,F.

claim: MAPK activation by Ca2+ requires EGFR signaling.
source: We found that EGFR RNAi completely inhibited ISCs proliferation caused by SERCA RNAi (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,F), indicating that MAPK activation by Ca2+ requires EGFR signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that EGFR RNAi blocks SERCA RNAi-induced proliferation.

claim: Transcription of the EGFR ligand spi was suppressed by trpA1 RNAi.
source: Interestingly, transcription of the EGFR ligand spi and the Pvr ligand pvf1 (Bond and Foley, 2012) were suppressed by trpA1 RNAi and up-regulated in midguts expressing SERCA RNAi in ISCs for 1 day to mimic early stages of Ca2+ induction (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Transcription of the Pvr ligand pvf1 was suppressed by trpA1 RNAi.
source: Interestingly, transcription of the EGFR ligand spi and the Pvr ligand pvf1 (Bond and Foley, 2012) were suppressed by trpA1 RNAi and up-regulated in midguts expressing SERCA RNAi in ISCs for 1 day to mimic early stages of Ca2+ induction (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and a citation to Bond and Foley, 2012.

claim: Transcription of spi and pvf1 were up-regulated in midguts expressing SERCA RNAi in ISCs for 1 day.
source: Interestingly, transcription of the EGFR ligand spi and the Pvr ligand pvf1 (Bond and Foley, 2012) were suppressed by trpA1 RNAi and up-regulated in midguts expressing SERCA RNAi in ISCs for 1 day to mimic early stages of Ca2+ induction (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Positive RTK signaling feedback loops may play a role in the activation of Ras/MAPK in the context of Ca2+ signaling.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that positive RTK signaling feedback loops may play a role in the activation of Ras/MAPK in the context of Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that RTK ligands are regulated by Ca2+ levels.

claim: Under homeostatic conditions, the basal activities of TRPA1 and RyR are required for maintaining cytosolic Ca2+ in ISCs to ensure their self-renewal activities and normal tissue turnover.
source: Under homeostatic conditions, the basal activities of TRPA1 and RyR are required for maintaining cytosolic Ca2+ in ISCs to ensure their self-renewal activities and normal tissue turnover (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is a summary of the findings presented in the manuscript, illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: Under tissue damage conditions, increased ROS stimulates the channel activities of TRPA1 to mediate increases in cytosolic Ca2+ in ISCs.
source: Under tissue damage conditions, increased ROS stimulates the channel activities of TRPA1 to mediate increases in cytosolic Ca2+ in ISCs (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is a summary of the findings presented in the manuscript, illustrated in Figure 8B.

claim: RyR acts synergistically with TRPA1 in a positive feedback mechanism to release more Ca2+ from the ER into the cytosol upon sensing the initial Ca2+ influx through TRPA1.
source: As for RyR, besides its potential to directly sense ROS, it is known to act synergistically with TRPA1 in a positive feedback mechanism to release more Ca2+ from the ER into the cytosol upon sensing the initial Ca2+ influx through TRPA1 (Pan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pan et al., 2016.

claim: L-glutamate and mGluR mainly affected the frequency of Ca2+ oscillation in ISCs, while their influence on cytosolic Ca2+ concentration was very weak.
source: Previously, Deng et al. identified L-glutamate as a signal that can activate metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR) in ISCs, which in turn modulates the cytosolic Ca2+ oscillation pattern via phospholipase C (PLC) and inositol-1,4,5-trisphosphate (InsP3). Interestingly, L-glutamate and mGluR RNAi mainly affected the frequency of Ca2+ oscillation in ISCs, while their influence on cytosolic Ca2+ concentration was very weak.
evidence: This claim is based on reference to findings from Deng et al.

claim: The number of mitotic cells induced by L-glutamate is far less than what has been observed in tissue damage conditions.
source: Strikingly, the number of mitotic cells induced by L-glutamate (i.e. an increase from a basal level of ~5 per midgut to ~10 per midgut) is far less than what has been observed in tissue damage conditions (depending on the severity of damage, the number varies from ~20 to more than 100 per midgut following damage) (Amcheslavsky et al., 2009; Chatterjee and Ip, 2009; Jiang et al., 2011; Karpowicz et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with published data, supported by citations to Amcheslavsky et al., 2009; Chatterjee and Ip, 2009; Jiang et al., 2011; Karpowicz et al., 2010.

claim: L-glutamate and mGluR do not play a major role in damage repair of the gut epithelium.
source: Consistent with this, in our screen for regulators of ISC proliferation in response to tissue damage, we tested three RNAi lines targeting mGluR (BL25938, BL32872, and BL41668, which was used by Deng et al.), and none blocked the damage response in ISCs, suggesting that L-glutamate and mGluR do not play a major role in damage repair of the gut epithelium.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNAi screen results showing mGluR RNAi does not block damage-induced proliferation.

claim: ROS can trigger Ca2+ increases through the redox-sensitive cation channels TRPA1 and RyR under damage conditions.
source: We find that ROS can trigger Ca2+ increases through the redox- sensitive cation channels TRPA1 and RyR under damage conditions.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The TRPA1-D isoform, which is expressed in the midgut, is sensitive to the oxidant agent paraquat.
source: In particular, we demonstrate using voltage-clamp experiments that the TRPA1-D isoform, which is expressed in the midgut, is sensitive to the oxidant agent paraquat.
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: RyR could amplify TRPA1-mediated Ca2+ signaling through the Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release (CICR) mechanism.
source: In addition, the results of previous studies have demonstrated the direct response of RyR to oxidants via single channel recording (Terentyev et al., 2008) and showed that RyR could amplify TRPA1-mediated Ca2+ signaling through the Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release (CICR) mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Terentyev et al., 2008 and established knowledge about CICR.

claim: Expression of oxidant-insensitive TRPA1-C isoform in the ISCs exhibits a tendency to induce ISC proliferation.
source: Interestingly, expression of oxidant- insensitive TRPA1-C isoform in the ISCs also exhibits a tendency to induce ISC proliferation (Figure 4H), indicating that ROS may not be the only stimuli for TRPA1 and RyR under physiological conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by mitosis quantification data shown in Figure 4H (note: text says Figure 4H but may refer to a different panel).

claim: ROS may not be the only stimuli for TRPA1 and RyR under physiological conditions.
source: Interestingly, expression of oxidant- insensitive TRPA1-C isoform in the ISCs also exhibits a tendency to induce ISC proliferation (Figure 4H), indicating that ROS may not be the only stimuli for TRPA1 and RyR under physiological conditions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that TRPA1-C can induce proliferation despite being oxidant-insensitive.

claim: Possible other activators of TRPA1 and RyR in the midgut may be irritant chemicals, noxious thermal/mechanical stimuli, or G-protein-coupled receptors.
source: Possible other activators in the midgut may be irritant chemicals, noxious thermal/mechanical stimuli, or G-protein-coupled receptors (Fowler and Montell, 2013; Shen et al., 2011; Zhong et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on citations to Fowler and Montell, 2013; Shen et al., 2011; Zhong et al., 2012.

claim: The concentration of cytosolic Ca2+ in ISCs appears to be regulated by a number of mechanisms/inputs including mGluR and the ion channels TRPA1 and RyR.
source: Altogether, the concentration of cytosolic Ca2+ in ISCs appears to be regulated by a number of mechanisms/inputs including mGluR and the ion channels TRPA1 and RyR.
evidence: This claim is a summary inference based on the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: TRPA1 and RyR have a much stronger influence on ISC Ca2+ levels than mGluR.
source: Although mGluR might make a moderate contribution to cytosolic Ca2+ in ISCs, TRPA1 and RyR have a much stronger influence on ISC Ca2+ levels.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of effects between mGluR and TRPA1/RyR on Ca2+ levels and proliferation.

claim: The extent to which different inputs affect cytosolic Ca2+ concentration correlates with the extent of ISC proliferation.
source: Thus, it appears that the extent to which different inputs affect cytosolic Ca2+ concentration correlates with the extent of ISC proliferation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that stronger Ca2+ effects lead to more proliferation.

claim: Cytosolic Ca2+ levels regulate Ras/MAPK activity in ISCs.
source: Although, as a universal intracellular signal, cytosolic Ca2+ controls a plethora of cellular processes, we were able to demonstrate that cytosolic Ca2+ levels regulate Ras/MAPK activity in ISCs.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi block Ras/MAPK activation in stem cells.
source: Specifically, we found that trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi block Ras/MAPK activation in stem cells, and that forced cytosolic Ca2+ influx by SERCA RNAi induces Ras/MAPK activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by dpErk staining data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Forced cytosolic Ca2+ influx by SERCA RNAi induces Ras/MAPK activity.
source: Specifically, we found that trpA1 RNAi or RyR RNAi block Ras/MAPK activation in stem cells, and that forced cytosolic Ca2+ influx by SERCA RNAi induces Ras/MAPK activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by dpErk staining data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Ras/MAPK activation is an early event following increases in cytosolic Ca2+.
source: Moreover, Ras/MAPK activation is an early event following increases in cytosolic Ca2+, since we observed increased dpErk signal in stem cells expressing SERCA RNAi before they undergo massive expansion, and when we co-expressed Yki RNAi to block proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by dpErk staining data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Ras/MAPK activity was reported to increase in ISCs, regulating proliferation rather than differentiation, in regenerating midguts.
source: Previously, Ras/MAPK activity was reported to increase in ISCs, regulating proliferation rather than differentiation, in regenerating midguts (Jiang et al., 2011), which is consistent with our findings about TRPA1 and RyR.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2011.

claim: The CanA1/CRTC/CrebB pathway is not likely to play a major role in high Ca2+-induced ISC proliferation.
source: The CanA1/CRTC/CrebB pathway previously proposed to act downstream of mGluR-calcium signaling (Deng et al., 2015) is not likely to play a major role in high Ca2+-induced ISC proliferation, as we tested multiple RNAi lines targeting CanA1 or CrebB and none of them suppressed SERCA RNAi-induced ISC proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic epistasis experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Deng et al., 2015.

claim: The active forms of CanA1/CRTC/CrebB cannot stimulate mitosis in ISCs when their cytosolic Ca2+ levels are restricted by trpA1 RNAi.
source: In support of this model, we also found that the active forms of CanA1/ CRTC/ CrebB cannot stimulate mitosis in ISCs when their cytosolic Ca2+ levels are restricted by trpA1 RNAi, whereas mitosis induced by the active forms of Ras or Raf is not suppressed by trpA1 RNAi.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic epistasis experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Mitosis induced by the active forms of Ras or Raf is not suppressed by trpA1 RNAi.
source: In support of this model, we also found that the active forms of CanA1/ CRTC/ CrebB cannot stimulate mitosis in ISCs when their cytosolic Ca2+ levels are restricted by trpA1 RNAi, whereas mitosis induced by the active forms of Ras or Raf is not suppressed by trpA1 RNAi.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic epistasis experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Paracrine ligands such as Vn from the visceral muscle, and autocrine ligands such as Spi and Pvf ligands from the stem cells, can stimulate ISC proliferation via RTK-Ras/MAPK signaling.
source: Prior to our study, it has been shown that paracrine ligands such as Vn from the visceral muscle, and autocrine ligands such as Spi and Pvf ligands from the stem cells, can stimulate ISC proliferation via RTK-Ras/MAPK signaling (Bond and Foley, 2012; Jiang et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bond and Foley, 2012; Jiang et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011.

claim: Multiple RTK ligands in the midgut are down-regulated by trpA1 RNAi expression in the ISCs.
source: We found that multiple RTK ligands in the midgut are down-regulated by trpA1 RNAi expression in the ISCs, including spi and pvf1 that can be induced by SERCA RNAi.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: High Ca2+ fails to induce ISC proliferation in the absence of EGFR.
source: Further, we demonstrated that high Ca2+ fails to induce ISC proliferation in the absence of EGFR.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic epistasis experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: spi is induced by EGFR-Ras/MAPK signaling in Drosophila cells.
source: As spi is induced by EGFR-Ras/MAPK signaling in Drosophila cells (Ammeux et al., 2016), and DNA binding mapping (DamID) analyses from our lab and others indicate that spi might be a direct target of transcriptional factors downstream of EGFR-Ras/MAPK in the ISCs (Jin et al., 2015) (Doupé and Perrimon, unpublished), the autocrine ligand Spi might therefore act as a positive feedback mechanism for EGFR-Ras/MAPK signaling in ISCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ammeux et al., 2016.

claim: spi might be a direct target of transcriptional factors downstream of EGFR-Ras/MAPK in the ISCs.
source: As spi is induced by EGFR-Ras/MAPK signaling in Drosophila cells (Ammeux et al., 2016), and DNA binding mapping (DamID) analyses from our lab and others indicate that spi might be a direct target of transcriptional factors downstream of EGFR-Ras/MAPK in the ISCs (Jin et al., 2015) (Doupé and Perrimon, unpublished), the autocrine ligand Spi might therefore act as a positive feedback mechanism for EGFR-Ras/MAPK signaling in ISCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jin et al., 2015 and unpublished data from Doupé and Perrimon.

claim: The autocrine ligand Spi might act as a positive feedback mechanism for EGFR-Ras/MAPK signaling in ISCs.
source: As spi is induced by EGFR-Ras/MAPK signaling in Drosophila cells (Ammeux et al., 2016), and DNA binding mapping (DamID) analyses from our lab and others indicate that spi might be a direct target of transcriptional factors downstream of EGFR-Ras/MAPK in the ISCs (Jin et al., 2015) (Doupé and Perrimon, unpublished), the autocrine ligand Spi might therefore act as a positive feedback mechanism for EGFR-Ras/MAPK signaling in ISCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that spi is regulated by EGFR-Ras/MAPK signaling.

claim: The cation channels TRPA1 and RyR detect oxidative stress associated with tissue damage and mediate increases in cytosolic Ca2+ in ISCs to amplify and activate EGFR-Ras/MAPK signaling.
source: In summary, our study identifies a mechanism by which ISCs sense microenvironment stress signals. The cation channels TRPA1 and RyR detect oxidative stress associated with tissue damage and mediate increases in cytosolic Ca2+ in ISCs to amplify and activate EGFR-Ras/MAPK signaling (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is a summary of the findings presented in the manuscript, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: A number of cation channels, including TRPA1 and RyR, have been associated with tumor malignancy in vertebrates.
source: In vertebrates, a number of cation channels (Monteith et al., 2007), including TRPA1 and RyR (Abdul et al., 2008; Büch et al., 2013; Du et al., 2014), have been associated with tumor malignancy.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Monteith et al., 2007; Abdul et al., 2008; Büch et al., 2013; Du et al., 2014.

claim: The findings could potentially help understand the roles of cation channels in stem cells and cancers.
source: Our findings, unraveling the relationship between redox-sensing, cytosolic Ca2+, and pro-mitosis Ras/MAPK activity in ISCs, could potentially help understand the roles of cation channels in stem cells and cancers, and inspire novel pharmacological interventions to improve stem cell activity for regeneration purposes and suppress tumorigenic growth of stem cells.
evidence: This claim is speculative about the potential implications of the findings.
